tagline: Build the applications and websites people actually use — and prove it with shipped work, not certificates.
what_you_do: You write, test, debug, and ship the code behind applications and websites, usually in an agile team: pick up a ticket, understand the existing code, make a change, get it reviewed, and get it in front of users. It's creative, logical work with a visible payoff. Be clear-eyed about right now, though: the junior market is unusually tough — AI tooling is absorbing the classic junior tasks and listings skew senior — so a public GitHub with real, shipped projects matters far more than any credential. Web development is the more accessible sub-branch to start in.
day_in_life: Pick up a ticket from the sprint board and read the surrounding code before writing a line
Reproduce a bug a user reported, then trace it down to the actual broken function
Write the fix plus a test that proves it, and open a pull request
Work through code-review comments — some picky, most fair — revise and merge
Give a standup update and flag the dependency that's going to slow this sprint down

salary.entry: Web dev is the on-ramp: median $90,930, entry ~$48,560
salary.growth: +15% for the developer group — strong long-term, but junior openings are the squeezed end right now
salary.note: U.S. BLS figures for Software Developers (15-1252) and Web Developers (15-1254); a median is the midpoint of everyone employed, so entry pay runs far lower — especially in today's tight junior market. Verify against the live BLS pages before deciding.

downsides: This is the toughest entry market in tech right now: AI is absorbing junior-level tasks and listings skew senior, so breaking in takes longer than the bootcamp ads admit. Interviews often hinge on leetcode-style puzzles that feel disconnected from the job. Imposter syndrome is near-universal, and the learning never stops.

fits_if: You love building something and watching it work
You can stay stuck on a problem for an hour and enjoy the moment it cracks
You're a relentless self-teacher — this field reinvents its tools constantly
less_ideal_if: You want a cert ladder where a credential reliably gets you the job
You get discouraged by rejection — the current junior market demands persistence
You'd rather follow fixed procedures than reason through ambiguity

skills.name: Programming fundamentals (one language deeply)
skills.note: Variables, functions, data structures, control flow — in JavaScript or Python first, not five languages shallowly.

skills.name: Git & version control
skills.note: Non-negotiable — every team runs on it, and your GitHub is your portfolio.

skills.name: Debugging & reading error messages
skills.note: Half the job is figuring out why code doesn't work — yours or someone else's.

skills.name: Cloud deployment & CI/CD
skills.note: Shipping to a real URL is what separates a project from an exercise.

certs.title: AWS Developer Associate
certs.reason: Only if you lean cloud-dev — proves you can build ON cloud platforms; never a substitute for a portfolio.

cert_note: Certifications matter less here than anywhere else in IT. No cert gates software development — hiring managers check your GitHub, not your credentials, and a public repo of real, shipped projects is the currency. Treat any cert as a late optional add-on, never as the plan.

trial.objective: Live the core loop of the job: build a small web page from scratch, break it on purpose, and debug it with your browser's developer tools.
trial.disclosure: Fully local — a plain text editor and the browser already on your computer; nothing installed or transmitted.

roadmap.title: Learn to code for real
roadmap.focus: Pick one free structured path — The Odin Project or freeCodeCamp — and go deep: HTML/CSS/JavaScript, then one backend language. Build tiny things constantly; watching tutorials is not learning.

roadmap.title: Ship a public portfolio
roadmap.focus: Build 3–4 real projects that solve actual problems, deploy them to live URLs, and put the code on GitHub with honest READMEs. This is the currency of the field — nothing else substitutes.

roadmap.title: Work like a professional
roadmap.focus: Learn the team toolchain: Git branching, tests, pull requests, code review. Contribute to an open-source project — it's real collaboration experience you can point to.

roadmap.title: Run the interview gauntlet
roadmap.focus: Practice data-structure and algorithm problems — leetcode gatekeeping is real even when it's unfair — and apply broadly, including web dev, QA, and support-engineering roles as legitimate on-ramps.

roadmap.title: Optional: lean into cloud
roadmap.focus: If your projects pull you toward backend and AWS, the Developer Associate cert can round out the picture — after the portfolio exists, never instead of it.
